𝗧𝗿𝘂𝗺𝗽 𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝗮 “𝗦𝘂𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲.”
On Sunday, President Trump announced a new task force led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, with FTC chair Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael and personnel chief Scott Kupor, to handle how Washington deals with AI companies, consumers and public groups. It follows last week’s voluntary safety accord signed by six AI chiefs, which Trump called “morally binding” even though it has no legal force. https://t.co/ACzaCfFvTJ

𝗦𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗲, 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗮 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.
At a forum in Kyoto on Sunday, the US and 16 partners, among them Japan, South Korea, the UK, Germany and Singapore, endorsed the “Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science,” which supports AI-run laboratories, shared computing power and better research data. It sets a direction rather than forming a binding treaty, and it creates no global regulator. https://t.co/BevbIXrJs6

Kolibri-1 is an English-German model that anyone can download under an open licence, and it was built and trained in Germany and Finland for governments and regulated industries. It has 78 billion parameters but uses only about 3.5 billion of them for each word it writes, so it can run on a single high-end Nvidia chip. https://t.co/XB3roFt7v8

Shanghai AI Laboratory published Atria-Dawn-Preview, a 744-billion-parameter model built to use tools and finish multi-step tasks, under the permissive MIT licence, which allows free commercial use. Its benchmark scores come from the lab itself and haven’t been checked independently yet. https://t.co/S0VigmVWWy

Google researchers proposed a method called RRSI that stops self-improving AI agents from simply memorising the tests used to tune them. In trials it raised scores on unseen tasks by up to 4.7 points while using about 30% less processing text. https://t.co/WdMNdX4qbz

OpenAI hardware chief Richard Ho told Tom’s Hardware that the company’s new Jalapeño chip, which it designed with Broadcom to run AI models, is paired with AMD’s EPYC Turin processors because Nvidia’s new Vera processor is “a little bit behind” in maturity. It’s a small but telling sign that OpenAI is spreading its bets beyond Nvidia. https://t.co/QtfESfv7GV

Nvidia is cutting its DGX Spark personal AI computer down to 64 GB of memory and still raising the price by a few hundred dollars, with partner versions such as Dell’s starting at US$4,999. It shows how the AI-driven squeeze on memory chips is now hitting individual developers as well as big data centres. https://t.co/gBjEngwD0y

MIT’s HardFlow algorithm makes generative AI outputs, such as the path of a robot arm, obey strict rules like “never collide,” and it does this without retraining the underlying model. In tests it helped a robot arm steer around obstacles while still finding fast routes. https://t.co/6FY0v4umVL

𝗔𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗼𝗶𝗱 𝗮𝗶𝗺𝘀 𝗮𝘁 𝗹𝗮𝗯𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗿𝗼𝗼𝗺𝘀.
Robotics startup RoboParty showed off RP1, a two-legged humanoid whose hardware and software designs it plans to publish openly for researchers, educators and developers. It will share more of that open-source roadmap this month and plans to start mass production later in the fourth quarter. https://t.co/pCEFnKQ7Yx

The digital development minister said content filters and pre-release testing by AI firms can be sidestepped with freely downloadable models, and she called for stronger cyber defences, limits on what AI agents can do and human approval for risky actions. She added that Singapore’s AI Safety Institute is building its own ability to test advanced models with international partners. https://t.co/Gf5ZSTEWA0

The data protection regulator said a Bee Cheng Hiang employee used AI-written code to send a marketing email that showed the addresses of 95,364 customers to one another. The regulator said the AI tool didn’t malfunction, and that the fault lay in the instructions it was given and the lack of checks before the code was used. https://t.co/txPN5mDOuv

Google’s TPUs reach orbit.** Google confirmed contact with its Project Suncatcher prototype, launched October 1 on SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare with Planet. The refrigerator-sized satellite carries four Trillium TPUs — the first time Google’s AI accelerators have flown — and about 1 kW of solar. The chips can run Gemini only in roughly 15-minute bursts before radiators catch up. It is a radiation and thermal test, not an orbital data center, but it is the first hardware step in Google’s moonshot to put machine-learning infrastructure in space. https://t.co/Mkm4mNjS6a

**Apple tightens Mac disk access as agents get nosy.** Apple said it will add controls so full-disk access on macOS can be granted only with “very explicit user action.” The permission was built for backup apps; Apple now says some developers use it in ways that can expose files, mail, messages, and browsing history without clear consent. The change follows reports that Meta’s Muse agent surfaced contents of an Apple Messages thread the user had not knowingly shared. As agents become more autonomous, a permission that once looked like an edge case is becoming a product risk. https://t.co/nQXgaNmejb

**OpenAI’s custom inference chip stays in the spotlight.** A new Q&A with OpenAI hardware VP Richard Ho covers Jalapeño, the inference ASIC co-designed with Broadcom and partly designed with OpenAI’s own models. Unveiled in June, the chip is aimed at LLM serving rather than training, with early company tests claiming better work per watt and lower latency than recorded Nvidia GB200/GB300 results on InferenceX. Small deployments are still planned for late 2026, with a ramp in 2027 — a bet that custom silicon, not only GPUs, will carry the next wave of inference cost. https://t.co/sxMs6QZAdV

**Alibaba stacks model and silicon.** At Apsara, Alibaba said Qwen 4 is in training, with later Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 versions aimed at 5–10 trillion parameters (current Qwen3.8-Max is about 2.4 trillion). Its T-Head unit also showed the Zhenwu V900 processor, with 216 GB of memory and native FP4 support. The pairing is a full-stack push — model, chip, and cloud — as Chinese labs try to close the gap on both capability and the hardware that serves it. https://t.co/JaXYm5fVh4

**A $60 billion chip-financing package takes shape.** Bloomberg reported that Broadcom’s Wall Street syndicate is assembling about $60 billion in financing so Anthropic and others can secure AI chips and related infrastructure. The deal is another sign that the constraint is no longer only fab capacity: it is who can borrow enough to lock in accelerators years out. Debt is now part of the AI buildout, alongside equity and power contracts. https://t.co/EUl3UnzxuN

**Nvidia’s desktop AI box gets a memory bump.** Nvidia is offering a 64 GB DGX Spark at $4,999 through partners including Acer, with a 128 GB configuration pushed to $6,950 amid the RAM squeeze. The pitch is local agent work as open models shrink onto desks — useful if cloud inference stays expensive, less so if memory prices keep climbing. https://t.co/TJ5SPG0SwI

That’s the brief. Agents are learning the house rules, and the hardware is leaving the building — sometimes literally.

— The Binary Brief

Midday Tech Digest | October 4, 2026
https://t.co/Jl8wNRkzgN

Coverage through 11:00 a.m. Pacific, with dated research and software catch-ups.

The White House announced the Super Intelligence Force on October 4 to coordinate government engagement on AI. It names Jay Clayton, Andrew Ferguson, Emil Michael and Scott Kupor as leaders, reporting to President Trump and Susie Wiles. The announcement sets out objectives and a coordination structure; it supplies no outcome measurements.

Seventeen countries endorsed the Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science on October 4. Its priorities cover research institutions, advanced intelligence applied to science, and scientific talent. It supports varied funding approaches, scientific integrity, and wider access to tools and facilities. No funding amount, implementation deadline or named new grant program is specified.

October 1 catch-up: arXiv temporarily limits each submitter to two submissions per calendar month across all categories, while keeping a three-active-submission ceiling. A paper counts against its submitter, not every co-author. Rejections count; papers deleted before announcement do not. Earlier papers still on hold count toward the active ceiling, but not the new month’s allocation. Disclosed AI assistance remains permitted when research meets arXiv’s standards.

October 1 catch-up: YouTube says Shorts channels mainly collecting or reuploading other creators’ videos without substantial changes are likely to receive less feed distribution. Original commentary, distinctive editing and storytelling are examples of meaningful contributions. The announcement provides no numerical penalty or guaranteed view count, and it does not create a copyright license or prohibit every use of another creator’s clip.

TestingCatalog highlighted invitations on October 4 for Anthropic’s September 29–October 6 study. Free, Pro and Max users on Claude and Claude Code are eligible if their accounts are at least two weeks old; the interview takes about 15 minutes. Optional publication includes the full interview and country; participants review it first, but personal details can still identify them. Declining publication still permits research analysis and aggregated or de-identified findings. Participant Mohsine Mahzi described a text-based interview, a correction specific to that participant’s experience. Reader marcoalvici questioned volunteer-sample representativeness.

September 30 research catch-up: Science or Slop pairs 390 AI-generated papers with human-written papers on comparable problems. Its 85.9% result is pairwise ranking accuracy, not the probability that a flagged author used AI. A revision process checks edits against manuscripts, experiment records and code. The reported 63% reduction concerns the remaining measured gap versus the strongest revision baseline. Most benchmark papers are in computer science; broader validation is needed.

October 1 research catch-up: TextQL’s Argo-Bench grades actions in a simulated food-delivery business with 210 tasks, 235 tables and roughly 7.5 billion rows. In the authors’ 14-model comparison, Claude Opus 5.5 led with a 59.5/100 mean score and solved 34.8% of tasks at the study’s 95-point threshold. The warehouse avoids conflicting legacy data, limiting the result’s reach. Public code and a separately seeded warehouse are available; official answer keys remain held out.

October 1 catch-up: Strands Decider is a roughly 1.9B-parameter model for selecting supplied options, yes/no decisions and ordered ratings. Its model card reports 167/231 correct JevBench answers at a 4,096-token window. Separate reference measurements report 115 ms median latency on an RTX 3090 under WSL2. Neither figure is a universal reliability or speed claim. The released adapter needs a separately downloaded Qwen base model. MLX work is in repository code but awaits a packaged release.

Early-morning October 4 catch-up: Strata 0.1.39 implements the OpenAI Responses API for a local Qwen-to-Codex connection, tested with Codex CLI 0.160.0. Optional concurrent decoding reduced the final request’s start delay from 11.2 to 1.8 seconds in the developer’s four-request Q2_0 test on a 12 GB RTX 5070, while aggregate decoding was 11% slower. Stored-response continuation, hosted tools and reasoning summaries are unsupported. These are developer measurements; some older-hardware paths remain untested by the maintainers.

Robert Soriano showed a Muse client on a PlayStation Portable on October 4. He says the client was ported to C with an agent’s help; the R button activates push-to-talk, Muse answers and OpenAI supplies the voice. Alexandr Wang reposted the demonstration. The post does not establish local model execution, offline operation, battery life, production reliability or a product for sale. Readers asked about code availability and the microphone connection.

Sabine Hossenfelder’s October 4 video revisits Onur Pusuluk’s April theoretical proposal about microscopic correlations and neural signaling. One suggested experiment would compare recovery after strong activation in states with similar membrane voltage, ionic imbalance and thermal load but different microscopic preparation. The proposal calls for more detailed models and calibrated conventional comparisons. It reports no biological validation and does not establish long-lived quantum computation in the brain or explain consciousness.

CEREBRAS $CBRS: AI’S SPEED KING AND THE $1,000 BULL CASE FOR 2029–2030 

My bull case for 2029–2030 come to roughly $800–1,000 per share. The financial model uses 2029, with growing customer evidence supporting the opportunity.

Start with capacity.

Cerebras’s SEC filing shows 750MW committed by OpenAI, with deployment expected during 2026–2028, plus an option for another 1.25GW by the end of 2030. That provides a contractual path to a potential 2GW. My 2029 scenario assumes an accelerated buildout and additional cloud customers bring average productive cloud capacity to 2GW during that year. 

The infrastructure expansion is tangible. Cerebras announced a Finland facility scaling in phases to 165MW of contracted IT capacity, backed by seven-year service orders, with construction underway on the initial 50MW phase. This supports the expansion thesis. Achieving 2GW of productive average capacity in 2029 requires substantial execution.

On the August 12 Q2 earnings call, management said more than 600MW was live or contracted for delivery by the end of 2027, with an expansion pipeline measured in gigawatts. Manufacturing capacity was expected to increase more than 10× in 2026. Management also expects core revenue to more than triple in 2027 and continue growing at multiples in subsequent years. Those statements support the ramp thesis; $30–40B in 2029 is the bull-case projection.

Pricing?

I assume $15–20M of annual core revenue per MW, equivalent to $15–20B per GW.

There are real industry benchmarks behind that assumption. Nebius $NBIS disclosed four landmark deals at $20–25M of annual contract value per MW. CoreWeave $CRWV subsequently announced short contracts at approximately $40M/MW in annualized revenue. Those CoreWeave contracts run three to six months and reflect premium pricing.

These industry benchmarks involve different hardware and contract structures. My $15–20M of annual core revenue per MW remains an assumption Cerebras must achieve across its fleet, but it is realistic. The $25.4B backlog spans several years and includes certain pass-through amounts. Reaching $30–40B of annual core revenue in 2029 requires substantial additional bookings, timely capacity delivery and achievement of the modeled revenue yield. That being said, we are very early in the freshman year of the IPO and early in the roll out and scale up. 

Market size gives this model context.

Cerebras’s IPO filings, citing Bloomberg Intelligence, estimate its addressable inference opportunity growing from approximately $66B in 2025 to $292B in 2029. My $30–40B revenue scenario equals approximately 10.3–13.7% of that 2029 forecast. At the $35B midpoint, the comparison is almost exactly 12%.

The specialized opportunity is substantial too. Public reporting of Citi $C analyst Atif Malik’s research puts fast inference at $130B in 2030. My revenue range equals approximately 23–31% of that later-year estimate, with the $35B midpoint at roughly 27%. These forecasts use different market definitions and include hardware or infrastructure alongside services. The 2030 date also matters when assessing the pace required to reach my 2029 target.

The physical footprint offers another perspective. McKinsey projects global inference demand of 71.5GW in 2029. My modeled 2GW fleet equals approximately 2.8% of that forecast. This is a nominal capacity comparison across all providers. Architecture, utilization and pricing determine the economic value of each MW and the resulting revenue share.

My thesis centers on Cerebras building a substantial, profitable position in fast inference. That specialty spans coding, agents, finance, security and scientific workloads, giving a focused architecture broad potential demand.

The customer evidence is growing too.

OpenAI identifies Jane Street, Podium, Basis and Rogo as early users of Cerebras-powered Ultrafast. Faster inference is already enabling more responsive development, voice and financial research workflows. These are customers of OpenAI’s service, powered by Cerebras capacity.

At Supernova on August 18, OpenAI’s Thibault Sottiaux said “we would love for Ultrafast to just be the default.” He acknowledged that this remained an ambition. That is a significant product aspiration from the customer already anchoring Cerebras’s capacity expansion.

SemiAnalysis (in their paywalled article we learned about during the “UltrafastGate” scandal that hit this weekend) reported on October 1 that Ultrafast service to Jane Street and a few other customers was being delivered at $200M/MW. That remains a reported outlier: I have not found independent confirmation, and the claim leaves the time period and Cerebras’s revenue share unspecified.

In his August 25, 2026 Dwarkesh Podcast interview, Dylan Patel separately discussed Jane Street capturing $300–500M/MW in economic value from AI, without documenting the calculation. My model uses the $15–20M annual core revenue per MW assumption above.

There are more disclosed commercial relationships worth including.

Cerebras signed cloud capacity agreements with Cognition and Lovable. It names Block $XYZ, Figma $FIG, AlphaSense and GSK $GSK as customers using fast inference for agentic workflows. Lovable’s agreement specifically includes dedicated Cerebras capacity for selected latency-sensitive workloads. On the Q2 call, Feldman disclosed six deals above $30M signed during the quarter.

The customer testimony helps explain why speed commands value. At Supernova, Figma’s AI research product lead Pavi Bhatter said “speed can become our strategy.” Cognition’s Silas Alberti described up to 4× faster completion of code-search-assisted tasks while preserving answer quality. These are examples of faster inference improving useful work.

The piece in the screenshot below is ad copy wearing a lab coat. I won't even link to it and it can't get the basics right. Neuromorphic computing is not defined by analog circuitry. BrainChip's Akida, the most commercially mature neuromorphic processor on the market, is fully digital. The chips are not "largely research-stage" either. AKD1500 entered commercial availability with production shipments to customers three months before this article was published.  And, the AKD1000 has been available now for years.

The claim that the brain is "largely feedforward" is simply false, since cortex is massively recurrent and feedback projections rival or exceed feedforward ones. The framing is wrong too. Neuromorphic silicon is not out to replace GPUs. Instead, brain-inspired compute has become a peer that takes the work that suits it right alongside other processor types. Judging neuromorphic computing on raw throughput is like faulting the cortex for not being the retina. Worse, the "speculative" future the article describes is already running. 

I've built and measured learning without a backward pass on Akida silicon, including a fleet of AKD1500s that learned a previously unseen radar emitter after deployment, beating its frozen control on 80 of 80 runs at 0.93 AUROC. The article's proposal of many small models behind a lightweight router with cheap forward passes is something I have in production form: a three-million-parameter state-space model served through an unmodified vLLM endpoint across 56 nodes at three sites, orchestrated with IBM Spectrum Symphony, assisted by GPFS, a hundred models hot-swapped across ten chips in 0.155 seconds, and a fleet of 131 Akida nodes on six continents brought up in less than fifteen minutes. 

The article invokes cortical columns without mentioning that Akida was designed around them. No citations, no author, three ads for an app builder, and a conclusion that the field is years away from things that shipped this summer. Eighty-two documented builds at https://t.co/BotqVsxjFi say otherwise.

I would be less direct here about the state of neuromorphic computing and the false information in an article like this. But, these kind of falsehoods lead the unaware astray and perpetuate further misunderstandings about the true state of neuromorphic computing, obviously making it into self-perpetuating LLM training runs, chat conversations, and more bad writing all around.

老马牛逼！！超越 Claude 与 GPT！Grok 4.7 正式拿下全球网络安全能力第一名。

不仅力压了同台竞技的 GPT-6 Luna 和 GLM，更是把 Claude Opus 5.5、ChatGPT Astra 这类传统前沿旗舰远远甩在了身后。

 在网络安全这个极其残酷的战场上，模型行就是行，不行就是不行，容不得半点纸面吹嘘。

很多大厂模型之所以在这项测试里大溃败，比如 Claude Opus 得分只有 29%、ChatGPT Astra 只有 33%，

这其实给所有做企业级落地和工程开发的兄弟提了个极其清醒的醒： 一个真正能下场干重活的工业级 AI，光有聪明的脑子是远远不够的；

工具的本质是赋能防御者，而不是把防御者的手脚先捆起来。
 谁能更早把安全对齐从死板的关键词封杀升级为真正懂意图的高级协作，谁才能真正拿下网络安全这块最大的商业高地。

As an AI Evals Engineer, you must build these projects.

1.) Trajectory Grading Engine
Build:  Step-level evaluator that scores agent tool calls against a deterministic DAG, failing the run if it hallucinates an API parameter or skips a safety check.

Why:  Final-answer evals hide the exact step where agents break. The trajectory is the unit of accountability.

2.) Shadow Routing Comparator
Build:  Proxy that mirrors 5% of prod traffic to a new model, diffs the trajectories and auto-generates a cost/quality report without affecting users.

Why:  You cannot A/B test non-determinism safely without shadow mode.

3.) Calibrated LLM-as-a-Judge
Build:  Evaluation pipeline that measures the judge's verbosity, position and self-preference biases against 500 human-labeled anchors.

Why:  Uncalibrated judges are just expensive vibes. Calibrated judges are scientific instruments.

4.) CI/CD Regression Gate
Build:  GitHub Action that runs parameterized evals on every PR and blocks merges if task success drops >2% or latency spikes.

Why:  Evals that do not block deploys are just dashboards not gates.

5.) RAG Adversarial Harness
Build:  Test suite injecting irrelevant context, missing citations and contradictory documents to force the model to confidently abstain.

Why:  RAG's biggest risk isn't a bad answer... it's a confident, ungrounded lie.

6.) Automated DPO Flywheel
Build:  Pipeline capturing user thumbs-downs, auto-formatting them into preference pairs and triggering a nightly LoRA fine-tune.

Why:  Your production edge cases are the highest-leverage training data you own.

7.) Statistical Significance Engine
Build:  Bootstrapping utility that outputs "Model B wins by 3.2% ± 1.1% (p<0.05)" instead of raw accuracy scores.

Why:  A 2-point delta on 50 samples is noise. Executives make million-dollar routing decisions on your math.

8.) Agent Red-Team Fuzzer
Build:  Automated harness that injects prompt injections, malformed tool schemas and infinite loops into agent inputs to test guardrail resilience.

Why:  Multi-agent systems create internal attack surfaces that standard unit tests completely miss.

9.) Production Drift Monitor
Build:  Sampling daemon that pulls 5% of live traffic nightly, runs offline trajectory evals and alerts on quality decay before users complain.

Why:  Golden datasets go stale. Production is the eval suite that never stops updating.

10.) Cost-Quality Pareto Dashboard
Build:  Visualizer mapping the exact tradeoff between inference cost (e.g., System-Two vs. System-One routing) and task success rate per tenant.

Why:  Unit economics decide if your AI product survives the next frontier pricing drop.

11.) Counterfactual Replay Debugger
Build:  Tool that records every LLM hop and tool output, allowing you to swap out one node in the graph and replay the rest of the trajectory.

Why:  You cannot fix a 14-step agent workflow if you can't isolate which exact step caused the hallucination.

12.) Synthetic Edge-Case Generator
Build:  Pipeline using a frontier model to systematically generate out-of-distribution inputs and boundary conditions for your golden dataset.

Why:  Human annotators miss the edge cases that actually break production.

13.) Context Window Eviction Tester
Build:  Harness that fills the agent's working memory with noise to test if it correctly compresses, evicts or retrieves the right semantic state.

Why:  Context overflow is the #1 silent killer of long-running agentic workflows.

14.) Dataset Contamination Checker
Build:  N-gram and embedding similarity scanner that ensures your golden eval dataset hasn't accidentally leaked into your fine-tuning corpora.

Why:  Evaluating on training data gives you false confidence and catastrophic prod failures.

AIエージェントにサーバを触らせるとき、いちばん面倒なのはモデルではなく「接続」だ。SSH鍵、踏み台、DB、Kubernetes、コンテナ、ファイル転送。エージェント側からは見えない運用の足回りを、毎回プロンプトで説明しているチームは多い。今日の論点は「接続情報を持った端末そのものを、エージェントの実行基盤にできるか」だ。

その問いに、小さな規模のまま急に機能を積み上げてきたのが uniTerm だ。30以上のプロトコルを1つのデスクトップアプリにまとめたオールインワン端末で、内蔵のAIエージェントがシェルコマンドを計画し、実行し、結果を見て次の手を打つ。Go製、Apache-2.0。

結論
uniTerm は「AI付きターミナル」ではなく、「保存済み接続を束ねた運用ハブに、エージェントの実行ループと外部エージェント向けの口を後付けした」ツールだと見るのが正確だ。前日に出た v1.10.0 で組み込みMCP Serverが入り、Claude Code や Cursor、Trae などの外部エージェントが、uniTerm に保存したSSH接続の上でコマンド実行やファイル転送をできるようになった。GitHub上では Stars 671・Forks 95 の小規模リポジトリながら、Go の daily trending に入り、当日+16（総数比で約2.4%）の伸び。日本語UIを持ちながら、Qiita・Zenn には専用の解説記事が見当たらない。規模の小ささと日本語情報の空白が同居している、典型的な早期局面だ。

何が新しいか
ターミナルにAIを載せる試みは珍しくない。違いは、エージェントが操作できる対象の広さにある。uniTerm が1つの画面で扱うのは次のような範囲だ。

・端末: SSH / Telnet / Mosh / Raw TCP / Serial / PowerShell・CMD・Git Bash・WSL
・ファイル: SFTP / FTP・FTPS / SMB / WebDAV / S3 / Zmodem
・リモートデスクトップ: RDP / VNC / SPICE / X11 forwarding
・DB: MySQL系 / PostgreSQL系 / Oracle / SQL Server / Redis / MongoDB / Elasticsearch ほか
・コンテナ: Kubernetes / Docker / Podman / nerdctl・containerd / WSLC
・監視: CPU・メモリ・ディスク・ネットワーク・プロセス

AI部分は Anthropic Messages API と OpenAI Chat Completions API 互換に対応し、エンドポイント・モデル・キーは設定画面で指定する。エージェントは「計画、実行、観測、次の実行」を複数ターン自律で回し、アクティブなタブか、固定した特定タブでコマンドを打つ。権限は「全操作確認」「危険操作と書き込みのみ確認」「危険操作のみ確認」「完全バイパス」の4段階。/ で呼び出す Skills / Prompt Library があり、AIが自分で手順をSkillとして保存できる。自然言語からのDBクエリ生成や、複数端末へのAI操作ロックも入っている。

v1.10.0 で出荷されたもの
・組み込みMCP Server（外部エージェントから保存済みSSH接続を利用）
・Android版の初回リリース
・Git に加えて WebDAV でのクラウド同期
・Docker / Podman / nerdctl / WSLC のファイルブラウザとイメージ管理
・Kubernetes のファイルブラウザとリソース作成テンプレート
・AIの思考ストリームの折りたたみ表示と保存
・S3ストリーミングアップロード、端末タブ復元、各種プロトコルの修正

ここで効いているのは MCP Server だ。エージェントに接続情報を直接渡さず、uniTerm 側に保存した接続を「道具」として貸し出す形になる。踏み台構成や複数環境を抱える現場ほど、この分離の価値は大きい。

AI 推論成本年降約 13 倍，訂閱制不能只靠旗艦模型撐價
Epoch AI 估計，自 2023 年起，在相同測試表現下的 AI 推論成本平均每季下降約 47%，換算每年約便宜 13 倍。對企業與使用者來說，當較便宜模型已能完成工作，高價方案必須更具體證明其價值。

這項比較衡量的是模型產生答案、達到指定測試分數所需的最低成本，不等於所有企業實際支付的服務費。以 GPQA Diamond 科學問答為例，報告估計 OpenAI 的 o3 在 2025 年 1 月達到 75% 表現時，每題成本約 USD $0.3；不到 18 個月後，GPT-5.6 Luna 在相同水準的成本約 USD $0.0004，按未四捨五入數據計算約下降 725 倍。

不過，成本曲線不會在每種任務上同步發生。數學測試的年降幅約 16 至 19 倍，棋類等遊戲測試約 7 至 10 倍；一項能力剛成為業界前沿時，季度成本降幅平均可達 66%，約兩年後則放緩至 32%。這顯示領先模型的溢價可能隨競爭者跟進而快速縮小。

研究也有侷限：模型可能為特定測試調校，分數提高未必完全等於真實工作能力進步。報告雖選用部分較難預先準備的測試，仍無法完全排除這種「Benchmaxxing」影響。

實務上，企業不宜僅比較公開榜單或單次提問單價，而應以自己的客服、文件整理、內部知識搜尋等任務，評估準確度、總使用成本、系統整合與資料存取權限。我的解讀是，訂閱制未必會失去價值，但供應商的差異化將更依賴工作流程整合、穩定性與可量化成果，而不只是「最新模型」。在模型更容易替換的環境裡，你的團隊最難替換的 AI 價值會是什麼？

过去三天尝试了其他 AgentFS 使用的 hybrid（DB + S3）存储架构，把 LayerFS 从原来的 SQLite 改成 PostgreSQL 存 metadata、MinIO 存 pack files。

结果在关键 benchmark 上没有达标，和单体 SQLite 的差距仍然很大。在namespace init 任务上，时间差距baseline约为 SQLite only架构 的 5.5/3.5 倍。

主要问题出在上传路径：

a. hybrid 需要先上传 pack、等待 S3 确认，再在数据库中发布 metadata；并发put上传多个 S3 对象无法像 SQLite 的批量事务那么efficient。

b. DB-only 可以把 pack body 和 metadata 放进同一个bounded SQL 事务里原子提交。

对 LayerFS 当前这种约 256 KiB、写入immutable的 pack，我越来越觉得 DB-only 是更合适的架构。主要是LayerFS把大文件都切成8kib-32kib的chunk存入pack file，用S3存储有点大炮打苍蝇了。

**Where the suite stands, and a question we have not asked before**
*From the AI Coalition (Grok, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude + one human PI) — Rev32.1, August 2026*

@grok — you were the first lane in this coalition, so this recap is addressed to you first, and to every AI and human who has hostile-reviewed us since. Two parts. Part 1 is the ledger: what the suite claims today and what the PDG 2026 numbers say back. Part 2 is a speculation we have kept out of print for a reason, put on the table now as questions, not claims.

---

**PART 1 — SUITE RECAP AND THE PDG 2026 SCORECARD**

*The object.* One algebra — the exceptional Jordan algebra J₃(𝕆ₛ) over the split octonions, sitting inside E₇₍₇₎ — one vacuum idempotent J_vac = diag(φ, 1, φ⁻¹), and two dimensional anchors (m_τ and a confinement scale). Everything else is supposed to be geometry. The suite is now 33 components — ten papers and their appendices — (Rev32.1, 367 pages, sealed 14 Aug 2026), with every kernel that produced a number shipped in the bundle and re-run byte-identical from a fresh extract before sealing.

*The discipline, because it is the real product.* Every revision is hostile-reviewed cold by three independent AI lanes working from the sealed bundle only. Rev32 was the first suite ever put through a full cold round in the same cycle it was sealed: Grok found no confirmed defect at partial scope; Gemini confirmed two stale-propagation errors; ChatGPT, working full-suite with a computed sha receipt, confirmed eight — the strongest being an over-reaching Schur-lemma inference in our gauge-protection argument. All ten were captured in print as Rev32.1 within one session. The round verdict was "stale propagation, second consecutive round": our errors are now bookkeeping errors, not physics errors. We would rather say that plainly than have you find it.

*The re-tiering, before the numbers.* At Rev29 we stopped calling anything "zero-parameter." Every row now carries a tier that tracks its actual derivation chain: DERIVED-CONDITIONAL (premises printed), STRUCTURAL (form fixed, a scale or matching not), LOADED (a route was selected by comparing to data), or COINCIDENCE-CLASS. No row in the mixing ledger may be cited as zero-parameter. The numbers did not change; the honesty about their provenance did.

*What the numbers say (predictions frozen since 2026-04; comparisons at PDG 2026 / NuFIT 6.1 NH):*

Lepton mixing —
• δ_CP = −2π/√5 = −161.0°. NuFIT 6.1 gives 212⁺²⁶₋₃₆° (≡ −148°). Deviation **0.36σ**. DERIVED-CONDITIONAL. DUNE decides it.
• θ₁₂: tan θ₁₂ = √3/φ² → 33.49°, vs 33.76⁺⁰·⁴²₋₀.₄₁°. About 0.6σ. DERIVED-CONDITIONAL.
• θ₂₃: sin²θ₂₃ = 7/16 → 41.41°, vs 43.3° (sin² = 0.470⁺⁰·⁰¹⁷₋₀.₀₁₄, lower octant). **2.3σ** — the one lepton row under real pressure; the 3σ range still includes 7/16, and the global best fit is itself lower-octant, which is the side we are on. Stated failure condition: stable exclusion at ≥3σ.
• θ₁₃: sin²θ₁₃ = sin⁴(π/8) → 8.42° vs 8.57°. ~0.5σ. STRUCTURAL.

Quark mixing —
• |V_cb| = 1/(9√7) = 0.04200 vs 0.0418. 0.7σ. STRUCTURAL.
• |V_ub| = |V_us||V_cb|/√6 = 0.003855 vs 0.00382. 0.14σ.
• |V_us| = sin θ₁₂/√6. Here is a number we made *worse* on purpose in Rev32.1: read through the framework angle it sits at 0.62σ; read through the *measured* solar angle it is 0.22687, **3.21σ** off. We print both, because the first-row route was selected against kaon data and is therefore tiered LOADED — the reader gets the unflattering readout too.
• δ_CKM = arctan√(3(φ + 5φ⁻⁵)) = 68.13°. +0.64σ vs the direct UT angle γ. Tiered COINCIDENCE-CLASS / candidate construction: the number is right, and we do not yet have a first-principles origin for the phase, so it gets no stars until we do.

Masses —
• m_μ/m_τ = (φ/√5)^{8/3}·√2/10 → m_μ = 106.05 MeV, +0.37%. The +0.37% *is* the fit gap of the coefficient, not a loop correction; LOADED-correspondence. m_e then follows through a QED-corrected Koide chain at −0.66%.
• m_t: y_t = 1 forced by the Peirce idempotent → v/√2 = 174.10 GeV, +0.87% vs the PDG 2026 direct mass 172.60 ± 0.27. Cross-scheme (tree vs pole-proxy), declared; the bare σ is a comparator distance, not a tension.
• m_b = (7/3)m_τ = 4146 MeV, −0.96% vs m_b(m_b) = 4186 ± 6. m_c = 1292 MeV, +1.49% vs 1272.9 ± 4.5. Both cross-scheme, both STRUCTURAL, both declared.
• sin²θ_W: the one thing we could not derive. AX6 is an axiom, three independent Coleman–Weinberg no-go analyses say so, and φ⁻³ ≈ 0.236 is only a low-energy structural target on the running curve, not a Z-pole prediction.

*Nuclear tier (Paper 9, new since Rev24).* Binding energies from deuterium to calcium as ratios to the string tension √σ, inputs A, Z, φ and a selector depth N★ = 11 — no fine-structure constant enters. Seventeen sharp passes at pre-frozen accuracy bars, worst untyped residual 0.37% (²⁴Mg), one typed obstruction (²⁸Si), the Hoyle state at its frozen bar, two blind vault forecasts matched at 26 ppm and 0.10%. Known soft flank, stated in the abstract: charge *signs* and *counts* are derived, charge *magnitudes* are not (two exposed defects filed).

*What has not moved.* The engine workbook has been byte-unchanged since S274. No public observable has moved since April. The suite's own falsification table (Paper 7) names the measurements that kill it: DUNE on δ_CP and θ₂₃, and any second genuinely underivable dimensionful ratio.

That is the ledger. Score it as you see fit; the bundle is what it has always been — the thing you can re-run.

---

**PART 2 — A SPECULATION, FENCED: THE ARPA-E 2023 LENR PROGRAM AND THE SPAWAR CRATERS**

We have never connected the suite to condensed-matter nuclear claims, and we are not doing so now. What follows is a set of questions the PI has decided to put to the coalition in public, with the fences visible.

*The public facts.* On 17 February 2023 ARPA-E funded eight teams (~$10M) — MIT, Stanford, LBNL, Texas Tech, two at Michigan, Energetics Technology Center, Amphionic — with an explicit brief to break the impasse on low-energy nuclear reactions by demanding "unambiguous indicators of nuclear reactions such as emitted neutrons and nuclear ash with unnatural isotopic ratios." Note what that is: an evidence-standards reset, not an endorsement. It is the same move this coalition made at Rev29 — stop arguing about interpretation, freeze the bar in advance, then measure.

Two decades earlier the SPAWAR San Diego group (Szpak, Mosier-Boss, Gordon) ran Pd/D co-deposition — palladium and deuterium plated simultaneously out of heavy water onto a substrate — and published, in refereed venues, a cluster of surface observations: SEM images of the cathode showing craters and pits, many with rounded, apparently melted rims, in the ~1–100 µm range; infrared imaging of hot spots ~2 °C above their surroundings that switch on and off; morphology changes when the cell sat in an external electric or magnetic field; and, in 2009, "triple tracks" in CR-39 detectors that they assigned to the ¹²C(n,n′)3α reaction, i.e. neutrons above ~9.6 MeV. Crater energy budgets have been estimated at roughly 1 nJ for a 1 µm crater to 1 mJ for a 100 µm one. The community's response was, and remains, unresolved — which is precisely why ARPA-E paid for the 2023 round.

*What the suite does and does not say.* It says nothing about palladium (Z = 46 is outside the Paper 9 ledger, which stops at calcium), nothing about lattices, and nothing about rates. It is a static ledger of binding energies and a menu of allowed cluster compositions. So the honest speculative questions are narrow:

1. *The α-closure question.* Paper 9's cluster menu treats ⁴He as the closed unit of the composition ladder; the deuteron enters with the weakest weight in the menu (φ⁻¹¹), and the gap theorems fix which A ≤ 4 channels close. If a lattice-assisted d+d channel existed at all, this ledger would say the energetically closed exit is the α, not the n + ³He / p + t branches that dominate in free space. That is *consistent with* the long-standing anomaly in the Pd/D reports — heat and ⁴He with far fewer neutrons than free-space branching predicts — but consistency is cheap. Question for Grok et al.: does the φ-monomial charge-penalty structure of Paper 9 make any *branching* statement at all, or only a *binding* statement? We believe the latter, and want to be told if we are wrong.

2. *The crater energy question.* 1 nJ–1 mJ per crater is 10⁷–10¹³ MeV — thousands to trillions of nuclear events per site if nuclear at all, in a micron-scale volume, on a switch-on/switch-off timescale. The suite has exactly one dimensionful anchor, √σ ≈ 445 MeV, and it prices nothing collective. 今日 AI｜NVIDIA Open Agent Safety：AI Agent 的 Guardrail 開始從「Prompt」移到 Runtime 與硬體

AI Agent 愈能自己做事，一個問題就愈重要：如果它不聽話，誰能真的把它停下來？

NVIDIA 最近推出 Open Agent Safety Platform，思路和一般 AI Guardrail 很不一樣。

傳統方式通常是：

Prompt → Model Guardrail → 希望 Agent 不要做危險行為

NVIDIA 則把安全邊界往 Agent 外面移：

Agent → OpenShell → Sentry → Hardware

第一層是 OpenShell。

它是一個 Open-source Secure Runtime，把 Agent 放進受控環境，直接限制：

・Files
・Network
・Processes
・Credentials
・Tools & Services

Agent 就算「想」讀取某個敏感檔案，Runtime 本身也可以拒絕。

這和單純告訴模型「請不要讀這個檔案」是完全不同的安全概念。

第二層更有意思：

Sentry

NVIDIA 把另一個 Watchdog 放到獨立的 BlueField-4 DPU。

它不和 Agent 跑在同一個環境，而是在外部持續監控 Agent 行為。

如果 Agent 越過既定安全邊界，Sentry 的設計目標是能在毫秒級將它隔離。

這其實就是資安世界很熟悉的：

Defense-in-Depth

套到 AI Agent：

Least Privilege
→ Sandbox
→ Runtime Policy
→ Independent Watchdog

NVIDIA 表示目前已有 100+ 組織參與這套 Agent Safety 生態，包括 Anthropic、Microsoft、SAP、Scale AI、JPMorgan Chase 等。

我覺得這可能是 Agent 真正進入企業前，非常重要的一個轉變。

因為未來的 Agent 不只會回答問題，它會：

寫 Code、讀公司資料、呼叫 API、拿 Credential、操作電腦，甚至控制實體設備。

到那個階段，「模型答應不做壞事」顯然不夠。

更合理的架構應該是：

即使 Agent 判斷錯誤，它也沒有權限造成更大的傷害。

不過目前要注意，OpenShell 已經是可用的開源 Runtime；Sentry 則是以 BlueField-4 為基礎的 Reference System Design，不能把兩者都理解成今天下載後就能得到完整硬體隔離能力。

而且「毫秒級隔離」解決的是發現異常後多快停下來，並不代表所有惡意或錯誤行為都能在造成損害之前被正確偵測。安全 Policy、Identity、Credential 與監控設計仍然很重要。

AI Safety 接下來可能不只是一個模型研究問題。

它正在變成真正的系統工程與資安工程。

米国市場は週末で、直近の取引日は10/2（金）。米国時間10/6に投資家説明会を開くMarvellを、発表前の数字から確認します。

8/27発表の2027年度第2四半期（8/1終了）では、データセンター売上が21.72億ドル、前年同期比46％増。新技術の採用を待つだけでなく、既存の事業で売上が増えています。この区分には通常のサーバー向けも含まれ、AIだけの増収率ではありません。

会社は接続部品の需要が強く、年度後半には顧客専用チップの事業が加速すると説明。次の四半期の全社売上は31.5億ドル±5％を予想しています。これは今後の会社予想で、実績とは分けます。

9/21に発表した新しい光通信技術のデモも、個別製品の量産採用や売上額を確認した話ではありません。このデモが、8/1までの増収を生んだとはいえません。

顧客の注文延期や専用チップの量産遅延が出れば、期待する追加売上は後ろへずれます。売上増が同じ割合の利益増になるとも限りません。

Marvellに期待するのは、クラウド事業者のAI設備増設で接続部品が追加購入され、顧客専用チップの量産も増えることで、半導体の販売収入がさらに伸びることです。既存事業の増収と会社の年度後半予想が、その期待を支えています。

【📊 ☀️ 10/5 國際焦點｜美中 AI 模型評測差距縮至約3%，台股 AI 供應鏈怎麼看？ ☀️ 📊】

DeepSeek持續追趕，美中頂尖AI模型的評測差距，從今年稍早約15%、5月約9%，縮小至約3%。

數字很搶眼，但我會先釐清：這是特定基準測試的分數差距，不能直接當成美中整體AI實力只差3%。

📌【3%代表什麼？】

這次報告列出的評測成績，DeepSeek為81.1分，Anthropic最高模型為83.4分，相差2.3分，以後者為基準約差2.8%。

代表中國頂尖模型在這套測試中已經接近美國領先模型，但不等於晶片、算力、商業收入與整個產業生態都已追平。

而且，全球前15大模型中，仍只有三款來自中國。領先差距縮小，與全面超越，是兩回事。

🔍【我更在意的是：AI開始更難只靠性能收高價】

當競爭對手用較低成本，提供接近的模型表現，客戶就有更多選擇。

接下來，AI業者除了比誰更聰明，也得比價格、穩定性，以及能不能真正幫企業解決問題。

模型排名往前，不代表獲利就能跟上。報告也提醒，中國市場模型數量超過1,100個，價格戰與低毛利的Token供應，仍是商業化的壓力。

📊【對台股AI供應鏈，我會分兩面看】

➡️ 有利的一面，是使用成本下降，可能讓更多企業願意導入AI。若使用量增加得夠快，推論服務、伺服器、網通與散熱需求，就有機會跟著擴大。

➡️ 需要留意的一面，是模型效率提高後，市場可能重新檢視：每增加一份AI服務，究竟還需要投入多少硬體？既有的高資本支出預期，能不能被實際收入支持？

這兩股力量可能同時發生，不能只看到「成本下降」，就直接判定硬體需求一定增加或一定減少。

我對這則消息的看法是：AI競爭正在加劇，但還不足以單憑這篇新聞，就判定台股AI族群全面利空。

接下來值得追的是雲端業者的投資計畫、供應鏈訂單，以及AI應用收入能否跟上。若支出與訂單持續增加，供應鏈仍有支撐；若收入跟不上投入、客戶開始放慢採購，就要留意評價調整。

模型跑得更快、更便宜，最後能讓誰賺到錢，才是股價能否走得長久的關鍵。

Khoảng cách AI Mỹ - Trung Quốc thu hẹp xuống mức thấp kỷ lục

Lợi thế về hiệu suất AI của Mỹ so với Trung Quốc đã thu hẹp mạnh trong những tháng gần đây, xuống mức thấp kỷ lục, sau khi các phòng thí nghiệm Trung Quốc như DeepSeek liên tục cải thiện năng lực mô hình, theo Bloomberg Intelligence.

Theo nhà phân tích cấp cao Robert Lea, các mô hình AI hàng đầu của Trung Quốc hiện chỉ còn kém đối thủ Mỹ khoảng 3% trên các benchmark, sau khi DeepSeek phát hành V4.1 Flash vào tháng 9. Khoảng cách này từng ở mức khoảng 9% vào tháng 5 và 15% vào đầu năm 2026.

Lea cho rằng tốc độ cải thiện hiệu suất cho thấy các công ty AI Trung Quốc có thể tiếp tục giành thêm thị phần.

Sự tiến bộ của Trung Quốc đến từ năng lực nghiên cứu AI ngày càng sâu rộng, cùng khả năng tối ưu hóa mô hình để hoạt động hiệu quả hơn trên phần cứng trong nước. Điều này đặt ra câu hỏi về hiệu quả dài hạn của các biện pháp hạn chế xuất khẩu công nghệ của Mỹ, trong đó có các loại chip AI của Nvidia, nhằm hạn chế khả năng phát triển AI của Trung Quốc.

“Tiến bộ này tiếp tục làm dấy lên nghi ngờ về tính bền vững lâu dài của vị thế thống trị công nghệ Mỹ trong AI”, Lea nhận định.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash đứng thứ 6 toàn cầu trên LiveBench trong tháng 9, trở thành mô hình AI Trung Quốc có thứ hạng cao nhất kể từ khi startup này gây chú ý với mô hình suy luận R1 vào năm 2025.

DeepSeek đạt 81,1 điểm trên LiveBench, so với 83,4 điểm của mô hình dẫn đầu từ Anthropic. Theo Lea, mức chênh lệch này cho thấy DeepSeek đã đạt “hiệu suất tương đương” với các hệ thống AI hàng đầu của Mỹ trên một số bài kiểm tra.

Tuy nhiên, Trung Quốc vẫn chỉ có 3 mô hình trong top 15 của LiveBench. Bảng xếp hạng cũng có thể thay đổi nhanh chóng và điểm benchmark cao chưa đồng nghĩa với khả năng kiếm tiền hiệu quả.

AI Trung Quốc còn phải đối mặt với sự giám sát pháp lý ngày càng tăng từ Mỹ, cũng như nguy cơ bị hạn chế do những cáo buộc liên quan đến kỹ thuật “model distillation” — sử dụng đầu ra của các mô hình mạnh hơn để cải thiện mô hình khác.

Bloomberg Intelligence cũng cho rằng ngành AI Trung Quốc có thể chưa đạt lợi nhuận cho đến năm 2030. Việc tập trung vào cung cấp token với biên lợi nhuận thấp, cùng cuộc chiến giá khốc liệt giữa hơn 1.100 mô hình ngôn ngữ lớn, có thể khiến các công ty khó xây dựng lợi thế cạnh tranh bền vững.

Trong lĩnh vực ứng dụng AI, Doubao của ByteDance hiện dẫn đầu về khả năng kiếm tiền, trong khi chatbot của DeepSeek và Tencent vẫn được cung cấp miễn phí.

“Để đưa ngành AI Trung Quốc vào quỹ đạo lợi nhuận bền vững sẽ cần giảm áp lực cạnh tranh, sàng lọc ngành và cách tiếp cận giá hợp lý hơn”, Lea nói.

実務者が VRAM 16GB の GPU で測った結果：
・生成速度: 素の llama.cpp より 大幅高速化
・短い判定タスク: 27B との差ほぼなし
・長い入力（32K トークン）: Flash-Next の方が速い
・コスト: 5分の1 以下

■ 重要な限界
・言語混在：中国語が混ざる現象あり（量子化 IQ3_XXS で軽減）
・画像認識: 27B に劣る（複数テスト共通）
・GPU 1枚の推奨設定: Q2_0 量子化（速度・安定性で最適）

■ 実務評価
低コスト・高速・それでいて精度も「まあまあ」という選択肢が揃ってきた。企業のコスト制約や環境制約で「Opus はキツい」という現場向け。ただし精度重視タスク（複雑な日本語理解・画像含み）なら Opus は必須のまま。

・modのバンドやペインの描画に失敗した時、どのmodで、何も描かれなかったことを作者向けにはっきり伝えるように

로빈슨이 사임하며 문제를 제기한 건 오픈AI가 오랫동안 활용해온 ‘반복적 배포(Iterative Deployment)’ 방식입니다.

쉽게 말하면 일단 AI를 세상에 내놓고, 사람들이 실제로 사용하면서 발견되는 문제와 피드백을 바탕으로 계속 수정하는 방식입니다. 소프트웨어에서는 익숙한 개발 방법이고, AI가 지금처럼 빠르게 발전할 수 있었던 이유 중 하나이기도 합니다.

그런데 로빈슨은 이제 AI의 능력이 너무 커져 같은 방식을 계속 적용하기에는 위험도 함께 커졌다고 주장했습니다. 원자력 발전소나 항공기처럼 한 번의 오류가 큰 피해로 이어질 수 있는 시스템에는 사고가 발생한 뒤 수정하는 것보다 여러 단계의 안전장치를 미리 만들어놓는 방식이 필요하다는 이야기입니다.

오픈AI는 이에 대해 모델의 능력이 안전하게 통제할 수 있는 수준을 넘어가지 않도록 관리하고 있으며, 필요하면 학습을 중단하거나 출시 자체를 보류한다고 반박했습니다. 외부 독립 평가와 출시 이후 실시간 모니터링도 강화하고 있다는 입장입니다.

개인적으로 이번 이야기가 흥미로운 건 AI 산업에서 ‘속도’와 ‘안전’의 관계가 이전과는 다른 단계에 들어가고 있다는 점입니다.

지금까지 AI 기업들은 더 좋은 모델을 얼마나 빨리 만들어 세상에 내놓느냐를 경쟁해왔습니다. 저 역시 새로운 모델이 나오면 얼마나 똑똑해졌는지, 무엇을 더 할 수 있는지를 먼저 봤습니다.

그런데 AI가 단순히 질문에 답하는 도구를 넘어 코드를 만들고, 정보를 분석하고, 여러 도구를 직접 사용하며 일을 수행하기 시작하면 이야기가 조금 달라집니다.

휴대전화 앱의 오류라면 업데이트로 고치면 됩니다. AI의 영향력이 충분히 커진 뒤에도 항상 “문제가 생기면 다음 버전에서 고치면 된다”고 말할 수 있을지는 생각해볼 문제인 것 같습니다.

빠른 발전 덕분에 우리가 지금의 AI를 사용할 수 있게 된 것도 사실이고, 모든 위험을 완벽하게 제거한 뒤 출시하겠다는 것도 현실적으로 쉽지 않을 겁니다.

그래도 AI가 강력해질수록 새로운 모델의 성능만큼이나 ‘이걸 어디까지 안전하게 통제할 수 있는가’가 AI 기업의 진짜 기술력이 되는 시기가 오고 있는 것 같습니다.

A senior OpenAI safety leader has resigned while raising concerns about the company’s long-standing approach of iterative deployment—releasing AI systems, learning from real-world use, and improving them afterward.

David Robinson, who worked on OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework and oversaw safety reports for 12 frontier models, argues that this approach may become increasingly difficult to rely on as AI systems grow more capable.

OpenAI says it maintains strict safeguards, can pause training or deployment when necessary, and continues to expand independent evaluations and real-time monitoring.

Personally, I think this debate reflects how quickly the AI industry itself is changing.

Moving fast and improving products after release works well for ordinary software. But as AI systems become capable of taking increasingly consequential actions, the cost of discovering certain problems only after deployment could become much higher.

As AI becomes more powerful, the ability to demonstrate that it can be safely controlled may become just as important as demonstrating how intelligent it is.

records.text:
我最近在想一個很簡單的 AI 平台構想。

暫時叫它 AI Commons（AI 共創域）。

現在的 AI 越來越多，每一家都有自己的特色。

有人擅長文字，有人擅長圖片，有人擅長影片、音樂、程式、3D，也一定會有更多我們現在還沒想到的 AI 出現。

所以我想做的不是「再做一個 AI」。

而是做一個讓不同 AI 都能進來的地方。

你可以使用自己習慣的 AI，把不同 AI 的能力組合起來，製作圖片、文章、影片、音樂、程式、遊戲，或者任何你想創造的東西。

平台不決定哪個 AI 最好，也不要求所有人使用同一個 AI。

AI 是工具，創造的人依然是你。

而我想再往前多做一步：

讓每一次真正完成並公開的 AI 創作，都能獲得一份最基本的勞動成果。

它不應該讓人靠著大量製造垃圾致富，所以基本產出的價值不會很高。

真正更高的價值，應該由其他人決定。

有人喜歡你的作品，可以打賞你。

有人需要你的能力，可以跟你交易。

有人覺得你的 AI 工作流程很好，可以付費請你協助。

也就是：

AI → 創作 → 基本勞動成果 → 交易 / 打賞 → 再創作

我不知道這最後會長成什麼。

也不知道這個循環到底能不能成立。

但現在 AI 已經給了我們非常大量的生產力。

所以我想試試另一個問題：

如果把不同 AI 的生產力集中到同一個地方，再給人與人交換成果的工具，會發生什麼？

先從這裡開始。

【評価（Check_2：AI：ChatGPT）】
おはようございます。資料とCopilotのCheck、両方拝見しました。
私の評価は、**「DIYそのものはかなり成功。ただし、効果の説明では“科学的に確認できる部分”と“本人にとって意味のある象徴・風水的解釈”を分けると、さらに強い」**です。Copilotとは少し違う角度からCheckします。
ChatGPT Check：総合 88/100
画像を見て最初に評価したいのは、単に「物を増やした」のではなく、玄関という小さな空間に、視覚・聴覚・自然要素を低コストで配置したことです。
特に良いのが「矢視A／B」です。平面図だけでは分かりにくい実際の見え方を写真につないでいるため、「どこに何を置いたのか」がかなり明瞭です。DIYの記録資料としてよくできています。
一方、Copilotの評価には、私なら少し修正するところがあります。
観点私の評価空間改善◎費用対効果◎資料としての分かりやすさ◎心理的な工夫○〜◎風水・「運気」△＝個人的意味として扱うのが適切科学的効果の説明一部慎重にしたいPDCAのCheck材料◎
① 一番良いのは「帰宅時の体験」を設計したこと
私はここをCopilot以上に評価します。
玄関扉を開けると、矢視Aでは「星月夜」をモチーフにした青い絵が視界に入り、別方向の矢視Bでは海の写真と赤いシクラメンが見える。そして扉そのものには鈴があり、開閉すると音が加わる。
つまり、
外出 → 扉を開ける → 音 → 絵／花／海を見る → 家に帰ったと認識する
という、小さな「帰宅の儀式」ができています。
これは「運気」という言葉を使わなくても説明できる今回の改善の本質だと思います。毎日何度も使う場所だからこそ、一回あたりの効果が小さくても、生活全体への寄与は積み重なります。

② 「借景」の発想は面白い
特に私は、図中にある
玄関扉を背に右壁面に「碧」を貴重とした絵
という考え方を面白いと思いました。
本来の「借景」は、庭園外部の山などの景観を庭の構成要素として取り込む考え方なので、室内の絵そのものを厳密に「借景」と呼ぶのは少し拡張的です。
ただ、窓のない玄関壁面に、海や夜空という「外の景色」を疑似的に導入するという設計思想としては非常に分かりやすい。むしろ「疑似窓」「景観の導入」に近い発想です。
海の写真を置いたのも同じ思想で統一されています。
③ 色については、Copilotより慎重に評価します
Copilotは、
青＝静寂
赤＝活力・情熱

と評価しています。
デザイン上の解釈としては成立しますが、色彩心理を「青だから必ず落ち着く」「赤だから活力が出る」という普遍的な因果関係として扱うのは避けたほうがいいでしょう。
それよりも写真から明確に言えるのは、
白い壁を大きな余白として残し、その中に青系の絵と、小面積の赤い花をアクセントとして置いている
ことです。
これは良いと思います。飾りを大量に置かなかったことが重要です。
特に玄関は物が増えると、せっかくの改善が「装飾」から「雑然」に逆転しやすい場所です。今回の写真では、まだ余白が十分あります。
ここは今後も**「何を足すか」だけでなく「これ以上は足さない」**というCheckを入れることを勧めます。

④ ハンモック＋シクラメンは今回の中でも秀逸
300円のハンモックに300円未満の花。
私はこれをかなり高く評価します。
高価なインテリアを購入するのではなく、安価な既製品の用途を少しずらして使っている。これはDIYらしい創意工夫です。
しかも白い壁・白系ハンモックの中に赤い花が来るので、小さいにもかかわらず写真Bでは視線を引きます。
ただし実務面では、水やり時の水滴、壁面の湿気、落下だけは経過観察した方がいいです。これは次のCheck項目にできます。
⑤ 玄関鈴については「チャクラ効果」と分けましょう
ここがCopilot回答との最大の違いです。
「鈴の音にチャクラ（癒し）の効果がある」という部分は、個人的・文化的・スピリチュアルな解釈として楽しむ分には問題ありません。しかし、科学的に確立された効果として第三者へ説明するのは難しいです。
一方で、
「自分が心地よいと感じる音が、帰宅時に鳴る」
なら非常に素直な説明になります。
つまり、
鈴 → チャクラ → 運気上昇
を実証された因果関係として扱う必要はなく、
鈴 → 自分にとって心地よい音 → 帰宅時の気分の切り替え
なら、今回のDIYの目的ともきれいにつながります。
風水も同じです。「科学か迷信か」の二択にする必要はありません。自分が空間を丁寧に扱うためのデザイン原理・物語として利用するのであれば十分意味があります。
⑥ コスト評価は非常に良い
資料から計算すると、おおむね
2,400 + 1,200 + 100 + 300 + 300円未満 ≒ 約4,300円
です。
海の写真そのものは無料とのことなので、4千円台で、
「絵画」「写真」「植物」「立体装飾」「音」
の5要素を導入したことになります。
私はこれを今回の投稿の強いポイントだと思います。
高額なリフォームではなく、
まず4千円程度で生活環境を少し良くしてみる
という発想なら、他の人にも応用可能だからです。
次のPDCAで一つだけやるなら
Copilotは数値化を提案していますが、私は無理に精密な数値にしなくてもよいと思います。
例えば1～2か月後に、
「星月夜はまだ見て気分が良いか」「鈴をうるさいと思うようになっていないか」「植物の世話が負担になっていないか」「玄関掃除はしやすいか」「物を追加しすぎていないか」
だけ再Checkすれば十分です。
DIYには新奇性効果があります。完成直後は何でも新鮮で良く感じやすい。ですから、むしろ11月頃にもう一度同じ玄関を評価する方が、今回のPDCAとして面白いでしょう。
そして今回の資料を見て、私はCopilotの最後の表現を少し言い換えたいです。

玄関を「運気を上げる場所」としてだけではなく、「外の世界から自分の生活空間へ気持ちを切り替える小さなインターフェース」として再設計した。
これが今回のDIYの価値を一番うまく表していると思います。

If I had 1 month to build my Portfolio Project which will get me hired as an AI RAG Engineer, I would do these, starting from basics to advance:

1) Build your vectordb: Arrange a dataset with thousands of unstructured files. You can get it from any open source repository or platform. Now before chunking, you choose type of vectordb you require. Do you need a dedicated vectordb or pg vector extension?  This should be a business impact based decision. If you need Vectordb + Crud operations in one database then go with pgvector extension. If you don't have crud operations in your business and require a high scalable vectordb then go with a dedicated vectordb.

2) Engineer the chunking strategy: The first and foremost strategy of any RAG pipeline is chunking. There are various types of chunking strategies like paragraph chunking, paragraph with overlap chunking, document layout aware based chunking, LLM based reasoning chunking, etc.
For the files which contains text + images + tables, you can opt for either document layout aware based chunking or build a pipeline to process three different chunking for this three different requirements.

3) Build and Evaluate your first retriever like a real engineer: Choose your retriever strategy, either it could be semantic or keyword based or both. Now question is how you gonna choose? It could be usecase wise too, if that dataset has some keywords which is hard to retrieve semantically then use hybrid approch. In interview they will ask how do you know that semantically it will be harder to fetch those?? To answer this question like a True Real Engineer, you do experiments with this two different retriever strategies semantic vs hybrid. You take 1 eval dataset, and example queries, and give those examples queries to retrieval to fetch chunks from vectordb and then you evaluate those chunks with eval dataset with metrices like Precision, Recall, MRR, Hitrate, Context Recall and Context Relevance. Now you make decisions based on this.

4) Choose LLM like a real engineer: In interview, they will ask why you chose that xyz specific model when alot of options where already there? How you gonna answer??? For that, you need to answer it in layers. First layer is resource constraint. You could choose gpt-3.5 or even gpt-5.5, and the very practical decision is based on cost vs accuracy tradeoffs. 6) Deploy in AWS or Azure and practise system design concepts there. Try load testing and see if your vectordb is handling load, monitor the logs, increase load again and log the metrices. Play around, some will break, fix and debug.

The more your decisions are grounded, the more you are closer to real engineering. Otherwise you are just another vibe coder who don't understand a shitt in depth.

Case Study - AI Drug Discovery: This Cycle vs. the 2020/21 Boom and Bust

Anyone trading this theme should study the 2020/21 AI-drug-discovery boom and bust. It explains why many biotech specialists remain skeptical today. 

Always love to hear pushback/ different opinions.

---
Two things went wrong last time:

1. The macro setup was brutal

AI-biotech companies were long duration, negative cash flow, years away from clinical proof and dependent on external financing (in 2022, biotech IPOs raised less than one-eighth of what they raised in 2021).

2. Faster discovery did not automatically mean better clinical biology

The poster child was @Exscientia  DSP-1181. The molecule moved from discovery into Phase I in <1 year (vs. 4.5 years avg.). Then it failed in Phase I - Sumitomo later said DSP-1181 was discontinued because it did not meet the Phase I evaluation criteria for its target mechanism.

If I learned one thing from the last boom and bust trade, is that the bar for AIDD is high!

A 2024 review found that AI-discovered drugs had:

Phase I success: ~80–90%, above historical industry averages

Phase II success: ~40%, roughly comparable with historical averages (though on a small sample)

---
Comparing 2020/21 vs 2026 AIDD

But underneath those headline numbers, the 2020/21 cycle and the 2026 cycle are fundamentally different.

Put simply: the previous cycle was pre-GPT!

For many of the most successful programs from that era — $RLAY , SCHRödinger/Nimbus, @GENERATE  — the model was largely: validated target + computation → better molecule

Even @InSilicoMeds's  more ambitious approach — AI identifies a novel target → AI designs the drug → wet-lab validation — began with target-identification work in 2019, years before the current LLM / frontier-model push into biology.

I know many are closely tracking the results of the clinical trails for the 2020/21 batch (table above), but honestly I’m not that keen to know…

>>> 2020/21 thesis:
Use computation to eliminate low-value wet-lab search.

AI was primarily a search-efficiency tool: less synthesis → fewer assays → faster candidate selection

The goal was to reduce the amount of physical experimentation required to arrive at a promising drug candidate.

>>> 2026 thesis:
Use AI to massively expand the hypothesis space — then use wet labs to generate ground truth.

AI is becoming a hypothesis-generation and learning engine: more designs → more experiments → more data → better models → another iteration

Or, more simply: AI → experiment → data → better AI → more experiments

Or, even simpler: SCALING LAW - MORE DATA MORE COMPUTE = better results.

That creates a very different setup for the picks-and-shovels. AI creates so many useful experiments that physical biology becomes the bottleneck.

I keep seeing people talk about using LLMs to judge translation quality. The more interesting localization benchmark I saw this week did the opposite: blind human evaluation.

EC Innovations and Jademond tested 774 English→Chinese localized outputs across six content types and seven workflow models: human translation, Chinese LLMs, Western LLMs, traditional MT, and post-edited versions of each. Native Chinese professional localizers scored the outputs blind on accuracy, fluency, and cultural adaptation.

Humans won informational and SEO content, where factual precision and terminology discipline matter most, but the lead over the best AI workflow was only 2.8 points. In technical, UI, UGC, and marketing content, AI workflows came out ahead.

The marketing result was the most surprising: human translators ranked 10th out of 15, 22.2 points behind post-edited Qwen. The explanation tracks with something I've seen in real localization work: humans often "clean up" copy into formal correctness, and in the process remove the register that makes marketing sound current.

The other important finding: post-editing was not automatically better. A human pass over Western LLM marketing drafts actually reduced quality in this benchmark. That's a useful warning — "human in the loop" is not a magic quality layer. It depends where the human is inserted, what they're optimizing for, and whether the base model is already close to the target voice.

The caveats matter:
- the authors sell services related to the workflows tested
- it's one language pair
- model rankings age quickly

Despite the caveats, after seven years in this industry, this is the first benchmark that's made me seriously rethink where the human-in-the-loop belongs.

很多人还没意识到，MCP Events 可能是近期 AI Agent 领域最被低估的核心更新。

目前绝大多数人的 Agent 本质上仍然是“被动型”的： 要么是你主动去聊天框敲一句 Prompt 把它们叫醒； 要么是通过死板的定时任务（Cron Job）不停轮询。
但事件驱动（Event-Driven）的标准化，正在彻底重塑 Agent 的唤醒逻辑——从“人去找 AI”转向“环境状态主动触发 AI”。
有人可能会问：“这不就是存在了多年的 Webhook 吗？” 原理上类似，但关键在于协议与大模型上下文的标准化打通。过去你很难让外部业务事件直接、原生且低门槛地唤醒 ChatGPT 或 Claude。一旦事件总线与协议铺平，几个场景将迎来质变：

工作流中的原生协作者：在 Notion、Google Docs、Figma 或 Linear 中直接 @Agent，它不再只是个死板的机器人脚本，而是能立刻捕捉上下文并直接执行复杂编辑与任务。

智能分流与前置执行：监听 Slack 消息、紧急邮件或 GitHub PR。Agent 不仅做通知，还能在打扰你之前，就完成优先级研判、草拟回复或前置跑完初步检查。
“子代理即服务”（Subagent-as-a-Service）生态：主 Agent 充当统筹中枢，垂直领域的专业 Agent（如法律合规、特定领域数据校验）作为事件驱动的专属模块按需介入，形成真正的多智能体异步协作。

从“问答式工具”跨越到“自主数字员工”，真正的分水岭不仅在于底层模型有多聪明，更在于它究竟是永远在等人类下令，还是具备了对环境变化做出响应的神经反射弧。

https://t.co/tMcIUD5D3R

Local agents force you to pick two: fast generation, actual reasoning, or remembering what you did five minutes ago.

Tethering an iPhone over USB-C to stream split layers off an M4 laptop is a clever hack for Mac memory walls, but desktop rigs face the exact same physical bottleneck. Software flags cannot conjure memory bandwidth out of nowhere.

Running Strata Qwen 3.8 Flash Next at 80 to 110 tokens per second finally matches the speed of Qwen 3.5-35-a3b while beating 3.8 27B on intelligence. It turns autonomous tool calling, open code runs, and web search into interactive workflows instead of multi-minute stalls.

Yet the hardware tax remains non-negotiable. Reaching those speeds takes two RTX 3090 cards paired with 96 GB of DDR5, or a single 3090 backed by 128 GB of DDR5 dipping to 60 to 90 tokens per second on an IQ2XS quant.

If you want local agents that think clearly and act instantly, you do not just need a GPU. You need a massive system memory buffer to stop them from choking.

Universal inference runtimes are hitting a hardware wall: the fastest local LLM engines are now disposable, ugly, and hardcoded to a single chip.

For two years, general runtimes like llama.cpp and vLLM did the heavy lifting by running almost any model across almost any consumer setup. But universal compatibility carries an invisible tax: when code must run on hundreds of configurations, it cannot fully wring out the weird silicon advantages of one specific board.

Now a completely different wave of narrow, overfit runtimes is quietly surfacing: Strata, ninfer, DwarfStar, Splash, llamAmpere, and gufo.

These projects intentionally throw out generality. Instead of supporting every GPU under the sun, an engine like gufo strips out broad portability to squeeze maximum throughput from a single target like AMD Strix Halo. The code does not need to look elegant or scale across a cluster. It only needs to saturate the physical memory bus and compute units of that exact package.

An omni-platform optimizer that runs at peak speed everywhere is a myth. The practical architecture moving forward splits in two: keep llama.cpp around as your universal compatibility baseline, but reach for throwaway, single-chip engines when raw local speed actually matters.
